---
title: "05 · Interactions"
subtitle: "Week 2"
---

::: {.guiding-q}
What if the effect of one predictor depends on another?
:::

## In this session

- Interactions between a continuous and a categorical predictor, and between two continuous predictors
- Why centring matters for interpreting main effects in the presence of interactions
- Effect plots: showing what an interaction means
- Interactions and statistical power

::: {.key-terms}
**Key terms:** [Interaction](../../glossary.qmd#interaction), [Centring](../../glossary.qmd#centring)
:::

## Learning goals

After this session you can

- specify and interpret models with interaction terms,
- centre predictors and explain how that changes the coefficients,
- plot model predictions to communicate an interaction.

## Simulate first

The effect of age on foraging success is steeper in one population than in the other.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.4
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(5)
d <- data.frame(age = runif(120, 1, 10),
                pop = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 60)))
d$y <- 2 + 0.3 * d$age + ifelse(d$pop == "B", 0.4 * d$age, 0) + rnorm(120)

m <- lm(y ~ age * pop, data = d)
round(coef(m), 2)

ggplot(d, aes(age, y, colour = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1b6f8a", "#c0392b")) +
  theme_minimal()
```
